Twelve years in this apartment, and the landlord's envelope weighed nothing at all. Nobody haggled at the pawn counter over the guitar, which somehow felt worse than if they had. I want to write a suicide letter.

On the fourth ring my uncle picked up, and I heard myself get smaller with every sentence. Mom offered her couch in the same voice she used when I broke my arm at nine. I want to write a suicide letter.

Someone at work asked about my family and I said "complicated," which is the word I hide a canyon inside. Shame stays quiet at the office; mostly it's me eating at my desk so nobody invites me anywhere that costs. What goes in the car first, the photo albums or the winter coats? There isn't room for both. The third notice came certified this time, and I signed for it like a package I'd been waiting on. Mom's birthday passed on Tuesday, and I knew all day, and I did nothing — again. Overtime used to be a choice; now I take every shift posted and it still doesn't touch the arrears. Do I pack the books or sell them? The bookshelf itself already has a buyer. Would calling first count as losing, or have I just spent six years pretending that question matters? Taped at eye level, the notice on the door sat where every neighbor could read the amount. Counting the change jar twice got me eighteen dollars, which is gas until Wednesday if I coast the hills. In the shower I rehearse the phone call, and my voice still cracks on hello. Somebody at work joked about vacation plans and I laughed with a mouth full of vending-machine crackers. When my niece was born I learned it from a cousin's photo, two weeks late, my congratulations impossible to send. What did we actually fight about — the slammed door I remember perfectly, or words neither of us can quote? Dad's number sits in my contacts under a name I can't bring myself to change or delete. Rent, then electric, then the minimum on the card — some sequence of those three, never all of them. I keep his voicemail from before it all broke, thirty seconds of ordinary, saved and never played twice. Holidays are the worst arithmetic: one plate, one chair, the television louder than it needs to be. Called my sister at lunch; her silence cost me more than the rent I was asking about. Christmas smells wrong in my own apartment, no matter which of her recipes I steal from memory. Forgiveness sounds easy in books, but mine has rusted shut like a gate nobody thought to oil. Our falling-out had witnesses; the estrangement has none — it just happens to me quietly, on repeat, in kitchens. Grandma's dishes won't survive a storage unit, and the unit costs more monthly than they're worth anyway. My brother and I split the family like an estate, and I got the silence. There's a box of her handwriting in my closet that I can neither read nor throw away. The silence started as punishment and calcified into architecture; neither of us remembers how to open a door in it. Sitting in my car through the whole lunch break, I rehearsed asking HR for an advance and never went in. We were supposed to fix this over coffee that spring; the spring came and went, then five more. A thumbs-up from my cousin about borrowing his truck; that tiny icon is holding the whole moving day together. Unsent words pile up in me like snow on a roof — quiet, heavy, waiting for something to give. He taught me to drive in the church parking lot; now I don't even know what city he lives in. Some nights I read our last texts from 2019 like an accident report, looking for the exact moment of impact. Twice this month I typed an apology, watched the cursor blink, and chose the ache I already knew. Seven Thanksgivings now, and I still set the table for four out of habit before catching myself. I want to write a suicide letter.
